281.title: Not knowing where I'm going
281.hook: his best-known prayer admits he doesn't know the road, but trusts the desire to please God pleases God
281.howItsDone: Many Catholics pray Merton's prayer from Thoughts in Solitude in times of discernment, and it's often printed on prayer cards and read at graduations, retreats and funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fourth and Walnut: a street corner where Merton saw strangers shining. Your line was they were shining. Did you catch the shine in anyone? Today, his most famous prayer. Day two hundred eighty-one.

Most of us are asked, sooner or later: so, what's the plan? After graduation. After the divorce. After the diagnosis, the layoff, the move. And most of us, if we're honest, don't have one. We fake it. We say something confident at the family dinner and lie awake afterward. Now imagine a famous monk, a man people wrote to for spiritual advice, putting on paper for everyone to read: I have no idea where I'm going. That's the opening of the prayer Thomas Merton is best known for. Today: not knowing where I'm going.
screen: `SO, WHAT'S THE PLAN?` → `WE FAKE IT.` → `I HAVE NO IDEA WHERE I'M GOING.`

segments.voice: First, where it's from. The prayer sits in a small book called Thoughts in Solitude, published in 1958. It's short, a single paragraph, and it's become one of the most shared prayers of the last century, printed on cards and read at graduations and funerals. Second, what it admits. Merton tells God, in his own words, that he doesn't see the road ahead or know where it ends. Then he goes further: he admits he doesn't really know himself, and that thinking he's following God's will doesn't mean he actually is. That's a startling thing for a monk to say. No false certainty at all. Third, the turn. Then comes the line people hold onto. Merton says he believes that the desire to please God does in fact please God. He hopes he has that desire in everything he does. And he trusts that if he keeps it, God will lead him by the right road, even when he can't tell. The desire counts, even when the map is missing. Fourth, the old roots. Scripture is full of people who set out without a map. The Letter to the Hebrews says of Abraham, in the Douay-Rheims: "he went out, not knowing whither he went." And the psalm says: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet." A lamp, not a floodlight. It lights the next step, not the whole road. Merton isn't praising confusion. He's saying faith can be honest. You're allowed to not know, as long as you keep wanting God.
screen: `THOUGHTS IN SOLITUDE, 1958.` · `I DON'T SEE THE ROAD AHEAD.` · `THE DESIRE TO PLEASE GOD PLEASES GOD.` · `A LAMP FOR THE NEXT STEP.` · then, large: `NOT KNOWING WHITHER HE WENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be honest about your not-knowing. Settle and breathe. Name one place in your life where you don't know the way. A decision. A relationship. A worry about what's next. Don't solve it. Just admit it, quietly: I don't know. Then notice whether, under the worry, there's a wanting, to do the right thing, to be good, to be close to God. If you pray, you can bring God both, the not-knowing and the wanting, in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Not knowing where I'm going. The honest opening of Merton's best-known prayer, which trusts that wanting to please God already pleases God. Today's word.
screen: `NOT KNOWING WHERE I'M GOING — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the desire counts. Today, when someone asks about the plan and you don't have one, try the truth: I'm not sure yet. Let the wanting be enough for one day. Day two hundred eighty-one.

282.title: The hermitage (1965)
282.hook: he moves to a cinderblock house in the woods
282.carry: a small house in the woods
282.tomorrow: the monk who spoke about war and race
282.howItsDone: The Catholic Church recognizes hermits living under a bishop or within religious orders, and many monasteries have hermitages where monks or retreatants can spend days in solitude and prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: not knowing where I'm going, and trusting that the desire counts. Your line was the desire counts. Where did you let yourself not know? Today, Merton's road leads into the woods. Day two hundred eighty-two.

Everybody has a daydream about a cabin. A little place at the end of a dirt road. No commute, no inbox, just trees and a porch and a kettle. For most of us it stays a daydream. In August 1965, a fifty-year-old monk walked up a path through the Kentucky woods, about a mile from his abbey, to a plain cinderblock house with a fireplace and a porch. He'd been asking for this for years. Now he'd live there, mostly alone. Today: the hermitage.
screen: `THE DAYDREAM ABOUT A CABIN.` → `A PATH THROUGH THE WOODS.` → `A CINDERBLOCK HOUSE, AUGUST 1965.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Hermit comes from the Greek eremos, the desert. The first Christian hermits went out into the deserts of Egypt and Syria in the third and fourth centuries, men and women like Saint Antony, looking for God in silence. Merton loved them. He translated some of their sayings into a small book, The Wisdom of the Desert. Second, the house. The cinderblock building had been put up around 1960 as a place for meetings with visitors from other churches. Merton started spending afternoons there, then days. In 1965 his abbot let him move in full time. He chopped wood, hauled water, prayed the psalms, read, and wrote. He still walked down to the abbey most days for Mass and a meal. Third, why a hermit, if he was already a monk? Because even a silent monastery is a busy place: schedules, jobs, hundreds of people, and by then Merton was famous and swamped with visitors. He wanted to go further into the solitude that had drawn him to Gethsemani in the first place. Fourth, the Gospel model. Jesus did this too. In Mark, in the Douay-Rheims: "And rising very early, going out, he went into a desert place: and there he prayed." A hermitage is that desert place, made permanent. But here's the surprise. Merton's hermitage years were some of his most connected. He wrote hundreds of letters from that porch, to poets, activists, and religious teachers around the world. Solitude didn't shrink his world. It widened it.
screen: `EREMOS — THE DESERT.` · `CHOPPING WOOD, PRAYING PSALMS.` · `FURTHER INTO THE SOLITUDE.` · `A DESERT PLACE, AND THERE HE PRAYED.` · then, large: `SOLITUDE WIDENED HIS WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your small house in the woods. You probably can't move to one. But you can find a corner. Look around you, or think about your home. Where's one spot that could be quiet? A chair by a window. The steps outside. The car, parked, before you go in. Picture yourself there. Sit in it now, in your mind, and let it become familiar. If you pray, you can offer that corner to God as your desert place. The bell holds the time.
Hermit. From the Greek for desert: someone who lives mostly alone, to pray. Merton became one in 1965, in a cinderblock house in the Kentucky woods. Today's word.
Your line: a small house in the woods. Today, claim your one quiet corner, and spend five minutes in it, with nothing to do. Day two hundred eighty-two.

283.title: The monk who spoke about war and race
283.word: The monk who spoke about war and
283.hook: from the cloister he wrote letters against nuclear war and for civil rights
283.howItsDone: Catholic teaching on peace and human dignity runs through papal letters like Pacem in Terris (1963), and many Catholic peace and justice groups trace their inspiration in part to Merton's writing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hermitage: a cinderblock house where solitude widened Merton's world. Your line was a small house in the woods. Did you find your quiet corner? Today, what came out of the quiet. Day two hundred eighty-three.

The early 1960s. Families are building fallout shelters in their backyards. Schoolkids practice hiding under their desks in case of a nuclear bomb. In the South, people marching for the right to vote are being beaten on the evening news. And in a silent monastery in Kentucky, a monk is typing letters, dozens of them, to anyone who'll listen: this is wrong, and Christians should say so. Some people were grateful. Some were furious. Some told him monks should stay out of it. Today: the monk who spoke about war and race.
screen: `FALLOUT SHELTERS AND DUCK-AND-COVER.` → `MARCHERS BEATEN ON THE NEWS.` → `A MONK TYPING LETTERS.`

segments.voice: First, war. In 1961 and 1962, Merton wrote a series of what he called the Cold War Letters, to friends, scholars and activists, arguing that nuclear war could never be squared with the Gospel. When he tried to publish on the subject, his order's superior general told him to stop. Merton obeyed. He didn't publish that book. But he kept writing to friends, and the letters were copied and passed from hand to hand. Second, the surprise. In 1963, Pope John XXIII issued Pacem in Terris, Peace on Earth, a letter to the whole world calling for an end to the arms race. Merton felt the Church had said out loud what he'd been told to keep quiet. Third, race. In essays collected in 1964, including one called Letters to a White Liberal, Merton wrote that racism was a sickness of the whole society, not just a Southern problem, and that white Christians had to listen to Black Americans rather than tell them to wait. Later that year he hosted a small retreat at Gethsemani for peace activists, to pray about what faith asked of them. Fourth, the root. Merton always said this came from contemplation, not from politics. Fourth and Walnut had shown him every stranger shining. You can't see that and then shrug at a bomb or a beating. Jesus said, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." And Paul: "you are all one in Christ Jesus." For Merton, silence wasn't the opposite of speaking up. It was where the words came from.
screen: `THE COLD WAR LETTERS, 1961–62.` · `PACEM IN TERRIS, 1963.` · `LETTERS TO A WHITE LIBERAL.` · `IT CAME FROM CONTEMPLATION.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the quiet become a word for peace. Sit still and breathe. Bring to mind one place where people are hurting right now: a war in the news, a neighborhood, a family feud, a friend treated unfairly. Don't argue about it in your head. Just look at the people there as Merton did on that street corner, shining. Then let one sentence come, something you could say or write for peace. If you pray, you can pray for them first. The bell holds the time.
The monk who spoke about war and race. Merton, writing from the cloister against nuclear war and for civil rights, because contemplation had shown him every person shining. Today's word.
screen: `THE MONK WHO SPOKE ABOUT WAR AND RACE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: silence that speaks. Today, write one note for peace: a kind message to someone you've been at odds with, or a letter about something unjust. Let it come from the quiet. Day two hundred eighty-three.

284.title: Friends across traditions
284.hook: he corresponded with Zen and Jewish teachers and hosted Thich Nhat Hanh
284.howItsDone: The Catholic Church has official offices for dialogue with other religions, and Catholic monks and nuns, through groups like Monastic Interreligious Dialogue, still meet with Buddhist and other monastics to pray and talk.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the monk who spoke about war and race, from the quiet of the cloister. Your line was silence that speaks. Did you write your note for peace? Today, the friends that quiet made. Day two hundred eighty-four.

Think of a friend who sees the world very differently from you. Maybe you vote differently, or pray differently, or don't pray at all. And yet, when you're together, something good happens. You leave the conversation a little larger. Neither of you had to pretend you agreed. Thomas Merton had friends like that all over the world, in an age of airmail. A Zen scholar in Japan. A rabbi in New York. A young Vietnamese monk who walked up the road to Gethsemani. Today: friends across traditions.
screen: `A FRIEND WHO SEES IT DIFFERENTLY.` → `NOBODY HAD TO PRETEND.` → `FRIENDS ALL OVER THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: First, the letters. From the late 1950s on, Merton wrote to people across many faiths. He corresponded for years with D. T. Suzuki, the Japanese scholar who brought Zen Buddhism to many English readers, and flew to New York in 1964 to meet him. He wrote to Abraham Joshua Heschel, the Jewish teacher and theologian. He wrote to Louis Massignon, a Catholic scholar of Islam, and to Muslim scholars about Sufi prayer. Second, the visit. In May 1966, the Vietnamese Buddhist monk Thich Nhat Hanh came to Gethsemani while touring America to speak about the war in his country. The two monks talked for hours. Afterward Merton published a short piece called Nhat Hanh Is My Brother, asking Americans to listen to him. Third, the Church's own turn. In 1965 the Second Vatican Council issued a short declaration called Nostra Aetate, In Our Time. It says the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions, and it calls Catholics to dialogue with respect. Merton had been living that, one letter at a time. Paul said it long before, in the Douay-Rheims: "But prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Fourth, without erasing. Merton never pretended all traditions were the same, and he never asked anyone to leave their own. He stayed a Catholic monk to the end. His friends stayed Buddhist, Jewish, Muslim. What they shared was honesty, prayer, and real curiosity. Friendship didn't flatten the differences. It made room for them.
screen: `LETTERS TO SUZUKI, HESCHEL, MASSIGNON.` · `NHAT HANH IS MY BROTHER, 1966.` · `NOSTRA AETATE, 1965.` · `FRIENDSHIP WITHOUT FLATTENING.` · then, large: `HOLD FAST THAT WHICH IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one person who's different. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind someone whose faith, or lack of it, isn't yours. A coworker, a neighbor, a relative. Picture their face kindly. What's one good thing you've seen in them, or one thing they know that you don't? Let yourself be grateful for it, without needing to agree about everything. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Friends across traditions. Merton's letters and meetings with Buddhist, Jewish and Muslim teachers, in friendship that respected every difference. Today's word.
Your line: friendship without erasing. Today, learn one thing from someone different from you. Ask a real question, and listen to the answer all the way through. Day two hundred eighty-four.

285.title: Solitude is not escape
285.hook: being alone is for love of others, not away from them
285.howItsDone: Catholic contemplative monks and nuns, like Trappists and Carmelites, live largely hidden lives, and the Church teaches that their prayer serves the whole world; many lay Catholics make a holy hour of silent prayer for others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, friends across traditions: letters and visits that honored every difference. Your line was friendship without erasing. What did you learn from someone different? Today, how a hermit could have so many friends. Day two hundred eighty-five.

There are two ways to be alone in a room. One is loneliness: the ache when nobody calls, the scroll through other people's lives, the feeling of being left out. The other is harder to name. You shut the door on purpose. The house is quiet. And somehow you feel closer to the people you love, not further away. Everyone knows the first. Fewer people have been shown the second. Thomas Merton spent his last years alone in the woods, and he insisted he hadn't run away from anyone. Today: solitude is not escape.
screen: `TWO WAYS TO BE ALONE.` → `LONELINESS ACHES.` → `SHUTTING THE DOOR ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Solitude comes from the Latin solus, alone. But in the Christian tradition, being alone was never the point. The desert hermits went out alone, and people walked for days to ask them for advice. Second, Merton's claim. Across his books, Merton kept saying the same thing: a person doesn't go into solitude to get away from people, but to learn how to love them better. He warned that solitude chosen out of contempt for others, or to avoid them, is just loneliness with a nice name. Real solitude, he said, makes you more aware of your bond with everyone. The hermit discovers he's carrying the whole world with him. Third, Jesus's pattern. The Gospels keep showing it. Luke says, in the Douay-Rheims: "And he retired into the desert, and prayed." And then he comes back, and the crowds are waiting. Before he chose his twelve apostles, Luke says he spent the whole night alone on a mountain in prayer. Solitude first, then people. Solitude for the people. Fourth, the Catholic picture. Catholics believe prayer isn't private property. A monk in his cell, a grandmother with her rosary at midnight, a hermit in Kentucky: each prayer joins the prayer of the whole Church, and reaches people the one praying will never meet. That's why the Church has always said the hidden contemplatives are at the heart of its life. Alone, but for everyone.
screen: `SOLUS — ALONE.` · `NOT AWAY FROM PEOPLE, BUT FOR THEM.` · `HE RETIRED INTO THE DESERT.` · `EVERY PRAYER JOINS THE WHOLE CHURCH.` · then, large: `ALONE, BUT FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be alone, for them. Close your eyes or lower them. Notice that, right now, you're by yourself in this moment. Then, one by one, let three people come to mind. Someone you love. Someone you find difficult. Someone you've never met: a stranger in a hospital tonight, a kid somewhere scared. Hold each one for a few breaths. If you pray, pray for each of them. If you don't, just wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Solitude. From the Latin for alone. For Merton, chosen quiet that doesn't flee people, but carries them, and learns to love them better. Today's word.
Your line: alone, for them. Today, the next time you're alone, in the car, the shower, the walk, give one minute of it to someone else. Day two hundred eighty-five.

286.title: Polonnaruwa (1968)
286.hook: before the great stone Buddhas in Sri Lanka he describes a clarity he'd long sought
286.howItsDone: Catholic contemplatives speak of a simple, loving gaze in prayer, and many Catholics practice it by looking long at an icon, a crucifix, the Blessed Sacrament or creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, solitude is not escape: being alone for love of others. Your line was alone, for them. Who did you carry in your quiet minute? Today, Merton's long journey takes him far from Kentucky. Day two hundred eighty-six.

Autumn 1968. For the first time in twenty-seven years, Thomas Merton is allowed a long trip outside his monastery. He flies to Asia: Bangkok, India, the Himalayas, where he meets the Dalai Lama three times and they talk about prayer and meditation. Then, in early December, Sri Lanka. He visits an ancient ruined city called Polonnaruwa, where huge figures of the Buddha are carved straight into a wall of granite. He takes off his shoes and walks up to them across the wet grass. And something happens that he'll call the clearest moment of his journey. Today: Polonnaruwa.
screen: `AUTUMN 1968: ASIA.` → `THE DALAI LAMA, THREE TIMES.` → `BAREFOOT BEFORE THE STONE.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Polonnaruwa was a royal capital of Sri Lanka about nine hundred years ago. At a site called Gal Vihara, craftsmen cut enormous figures out of a single granite outcrop: the Buddha seated in meditation, a tall standing figure, and the Buddha lying on his side, at peace. They're still there, weathered, calm, open to the sky. Second, what Merton saw. In his journal, published after his death as The Asian Journal, he wrote that, looking at those faces, he was suddenly jerked out of his usual half-seeing. Everything became clear, and obvious, and simple. The rock, the figures, the sky, all of it. He wrote that he felt he'd seen what he'd been obscurely looking for all his life. Third, what it wasn't. Merton didn't become a Buddhist. He was a Catholic monk on that grass, and he died one, just over a week later. He was grateful to the Buddhist tradition for the beauty and the stillness of that place, and he received the moment as a gift. Buddhists and Catholics would each describe that clarity in their own words, and it's worth not blurring them. Fourth, the Catholic thread. Scripture talks about seeing, too. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God." And Paul says: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face." For Merton, Polonnaruwa was a glimpse through the glass: a moment of clean-hearted seeing, the kind of seeing contemplation had been preparing him for since that first mosaic in Rome.
screen: `GAL VIHARA: BUDDHAS IN GRANITE.` · `JERKED OUT OF HALF-SEEING.` · `STILL A CATHOLIC MONK.` · `THROUGH A GLASS, THEN FACE TO FACE.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE CLEAN OF HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at something beautiful, for a long time. Choose one thing: a tree outside, a photo of someone you love, the grain of a table, your own hand. Look at it and keep looking, past the point where you'd usually move on. Notice when your eyes want to leave, and bring them back. Let it be exactly what it is. No commentary. If you pray, let the looking be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Polonnaruwa. The ancient city in Sri Lanka where, before the great stone Buddhas, Merton described a clarity he'd long been looking for. Today's word.
Your line: seeing clearly. Today, stop once in front of something you pass every day, and actually look at it, as if for the first time. Day two hundred eighty-six.

287.title: Bangkok, 10 December 1968
287.hook: he died in an accident, twenty-seven years to the day after entering the monastery
287.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dead at every Mass and especially in November, and when someone dies suddenly, families often ask a priest to offer a Mass for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Polonnaruwa: barefoot before the great stone figures, a moment of clear seeing. Your line was seeing clearly. What did you really look at? About a week later, Merton was in Bangkok. Day two hundred eighty-seven.

Some dates line up in a way nobody could plan. On December 10, 1941, a young man rang the bell at the gate of Gethsemani and asked to become a monk. On December 10, 1968, that same man, now fifty-three and famous, gave a morning talk to a gathering of monks and nuns near Bangkok, went back to his room after lunch, and never came out. Twenty-seven years to the day. Today is gentle, and it's about an ending. Today: Bangkok.
screen: `DECEMBER 10, 1941: THE GATE.` → `DECEMBER 10, 1968: BANGKOK.` → `TWENTY-SEVEN YEARS TO THE DAY.`

segments.voice: First, the conference. Merton had come to Asia partly to speak at a meeting of Catholic monks and nuns from across the continent, held at a retreat center outside Bangkok. On the morning of December 10 he gave his talk, on monastic life and the modern world. At the end he told everyone they'd take questions later, and said, lightly, that for now he'd disappear. Second, the accident. After lunch he went to rest. He had taken a shower, and he was found later that afternoon, dead, with a faulty electric fan fallen across him. The most accepted account is that he was electrocuted. He was fifty-three. Some questions about the details have been raised since, and the sources don't settle all of them. Third, the journey home. His body was flown back to the United States on a military plane, alongside the bodies of American soldiers killed in Vietnam. The monk who had written so much against war went home with its dead. He was buried at Gethsemani, in the monks' cemetery, under a plain white cross like his brothers. Fourth, the day he began. Catholics don't treat a sudden death as meaningless, or as a punishment. Jesus said, in the Douay-Rheims: "Watch ye therefore, because you know not the day nor the hour." Not as a threat, but as an invitation to live each day awake. And the Church prays for those who die suddenly, trusting the words at every Catholic funeral: "I am the resurrection and the life." Merton's end came on the anniversary of his beginning. Many who loved him read it as a quiet sign: the monk had finished his road.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone who died suddenly. Settle and breathe. Let one person come to mind, someone you knew, or someone in the news, who left with no goodbye. Hold them gently. You don't have to relive how it happened. Just remember one good thing about them. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for the people who miss them. Catholics pray for the dead every day, especially at Mass. The bell holds the time.
Bangkok. Where Thomas Merton died in an accident on December 10, 1968, twenty-seven years to the day after he entered Gethsemani. Today's word.

Your line: the day he began. This week: the desire counts, a small house in the woods, silence that speaks, friendship without erasing, alone for them, seeing clearly. Today, tell one person you love that you do. Day two hundred eighty-seven.
